659.title: Before you were a thing
659.hook: was there a time when the human was nothing worth mentioning (76:1)
659.howItsDone: Surah al-Insan (also called ad-Dahr) is recited in some mosques in the dawn prayer on Fridays, alongside as-Sajdah, following the Prophet's practice reported in Bukhari and Muslim.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jibril, and don't hurry your tongue, and your line, don't hurry. Did someone get to finish their sentence before you spoke? Today a new surah, named for us: al-Insan, the Human. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

Find a photo from before you were born. Your parents' wedding, maybe, or a family picnic. Everyone's there, laughing, squinting into the sun. The world is going on, full of people and plans and weather. And you're nowhere. Not hiding, not waiting offstage. Just not yet. Nobody in the picture is thinking of you, because there is no you yet to think of. Surah seventy-six opens by asking us to think about it on purpose, with a question that isn't really a question.

Verse one, in Pickthall's translation: "Hath there come upon man (ever) any period of time in which he was a thing unremembered?" The Arabic phrase at the end is shay'an madhkura: a thing mentioned, a thing worth speaking of. There was a stretch of time, the verse says, when the human being wasn't even that. Not a name, not a memory, not a thought in anyone's head. Some commentators point out that the opening word, hal, usually a question, works here more like a statement: indeed, there came such a time. The answer is built into the asking. Of course there was. Then verse two moves fast: We created the human from a drop, mingled, to test him, and We made him hearing, seeing. From nothing worth mentioning, to a drop, to a listener and a watcher. And verse three: We showed him the way, whether he is grateful or ungrateful. The surah has a second name, ad-Dahr, Time, after this first verse. And it has a special place in the week. According to hadith in Bukhari and Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would recite it, along with surah as-Sajdah, in the dawn prayer on Fridays, and some mosques keep that custom. Where they do, the congregation begins Friday by remembering it was once nothing. Why start there? Because it reframes everything that follows. If you were once not even a thing mentioned, then everything since, your breath, your name, the people in your life, the very ability to hear these words, arrived as a gift. Gratitude starts from zero.

The practice: think of before you were born. Sit, and picture the world a year before you arrived. The same sky, the same streets, maybe your parents young. You aren't in it. Stay with that for a few breaths, without fear. Then, slowly, add yourself back: your first breath, your name being said for the first time, your eyes opening, your ears hearing. Notice each one as something that arrived. The bell holds the time.
Shay'an madhkura. A thing worth mentioning: in 76:1 the Qur'an recalls a time when the human wasn't even that, before being made hearing and seeing. Today's word.
Your line: once, nothing. Today, when you catch yourself taking something for granted, your hands, your hearing, a person, remember it wasn't always there. Day six hundred fifty-nine.

660.title: For love of Him
660.hook: they feed the poor, the orphan and the captive, for His sake, wanting no thanks (76:8–9)
660.howItsDone: Feeding the hungry is praised in the Qur'an and hadith; Muslims give food in Ramadan and through the year, and 76:8–9 is cited for giving for Allah's sake alone, without seeking thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shay'an madhkura, and your line, once, nothing. Did something you take for granted look like a gift? Today al-Insan shows what grateful people do with their hands. Day six hundred sixty.

A family at sunset, about to eat for the first time all day. The bread is on the table. Then a knock. Someone outside is hungry. They hand over the bread. The next evening, another knock, another hungry person. The bread goes again. And the third night, a third. They go to bed with empty stomachs, three nights running. There's a story like this, told about a family very close to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. It's linked to a few verses in surah al-Insan.

Verses eight and nine, in Pickthall's translation: "And feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him, (Saying): We feed you, for the sake of Allah only. We wish for no reward nor thanks from you." Three people at the door. The poor, the orphan, and the captive. Commentators note that in the Prophet's time a captive could be a prisoner of war who was not a Muslim, and the verse praises feeding them too: hunger doesn't check anyone's religion. Now, a puzzle in two words. 'Ala hubbihi. Pickthall says: for love of Him, meaning Allah. But the Arabic pronoun could also point to the food: they feed others despite their love of it, while they want it themselves. Commentators have defended both readings, and some say both are true. Either way, the giving costs something. Then the line that names the attitude: we want no reward from you, and no thanks. Not even a thank-you. And the family at the door? Shia Muslims, and a number of Sunni commentators, hold that these verses came down about 'Ali, Fatimah, and their sons Hasan and Husayn, who fasted three days and gave their bread away each night to a poor man, an orphan, and a captive. Shia tradition treats this as firmly established. Other Sunni scholars question the chain of that report, and read the verses as describing the righteous in general. Both read the same verses with deep respect. And in both readings, the people at the door never even had to say thank you.
screen: `FOR LOVE OF HIM, OR OF THE FOOD?`

segments.voice: The practice: feed someone and refuse thanks. Sit, and think of a food you actually love, not leftovers, not the thing you'd throw out. That's 'ala hubbihi: giving what you'd like for yourself. Now think of who you could share it with today or this week: a neighbor, a coworker, someone on the street, a food bank. Picture handing it over, and when the thank-you starts, letting it pass: no need. Plan the real thing. The bell holds the time.
'Ala hubbihi. For love of Him, or despite love of the food: two readings of 76:8–9, where the righteous feed the poor for Allah's sake alone. Today's word.
Your line: no thanks wanted. Today, feed someone, a meal, a snack, a coffee, and when the thanks comes, let it pass without collecting it. Day six hundred sixty.

661.title: Morning and evening
661.hook: remember your Lord's name morning and evening, and prostrate at night (76:25–26)
661.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the adhkar of the morning and evening, short remembrances, verses and prayers, after the dawn prayer and around sunset, often from a small booklet or from memory, following 76:25, 33:42 and many hadith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'ala hubbihi, and your line, no thanks wanted. Did someone get fed, and did you let the thanks pass? Today, our last day in al-Insan, and the two hinges of every day. Day six hundred sixty-one.

Every day has two doors. The one you walk out of in the morning, keys in hand, coffee half finished. And the one you walk back through in the evening, shoes off, bag dropped, the day behind you. Most of us cross both without noticing, already thinking about the next thing. Near the end of surah al-Insan, after its long picture of a garden for the grateful, the Qur'an gives the Prophet a short instruction about those two doors.
screen: `OUT IN THE MORNING, IN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-five, in Pickthall's translation: "Remember the name of thy Lord at morn and evening." The Arabic is bukratan wa asila. Bukrah is the early morning, the first hours. Asil is the late afternoon into evening, as the light goes gold. Then verse twenty-six: and part of the night, prostrate to Him, and glorify Him through a long night. So the day gets framed. Begin with His name. End with His name. Give some of the dark to prayer. Commentators connect these times to the daily prayers, the dawn prayer, the afternoon and evening prayers, and the night prayer. And the Qur'an uses the same pairing elsewhere: in surah al-Ahzab, believers are told to remember Allah often, and glorify Him morning and evening. From these verses and many hadith grew a whole practice that millions of Muslims keep: the adhkar of the morning and the evening. Short remembrances, said after the dawn prayer and again before or after sunset. There are phrases of praise, verses like Ayat al-Kursi and the last three surahs, and a prayer for forgiveness that a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari calls the master of all prayers for forgiveness, to be said morning and evening. Some people say them from a small booklet; some from memory, walking to the bus. Why the two ends of the day? Because those are the hinges. What you say as the door opens sets the tone for whatever comes through it. And what you say as it closes decides what you carry into sleep. The middle of the day will be busy. The edges can be held.
screen: `BEGIN WITH HIS NAME, END WITH IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: adhkar, morning and evening remembered. Sit, and choose one short line you'll say at both doors of tomorrow. If you pray, it might be bismillah, or subhanallah, or alhamdulillah, or the name of your Lord, said slowly. If you don't, it might be a single breath of thanks. Now picture tomorrow's first door, and say the line there. Then picture tomorrow's last door, and say it again. The bell holds the time.
Adhkar. The morning and evening remembrances in 76:25's bukratan wa asila, short phrases of praise said at the two edges of the day. Today's word.
Your line: the edges can be held. Tonight, as you come through the last door of the day, say your line once. Tomorrow, say it again on the way out. Day six hundred sixty-one.

662.title: Those sent forth
662.hook: by the winds sent forth one after another (77:1)
662.howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is a short Meccan surah recited in prayer; commentators differ on whether its first verses describe winds, angels or both.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Insan, and your line: the edges can be held. Did the name of your Lord, or just a quiet pause, come at both ends of the day? Today a new surah, al-Mursalat. Day six hundred sixty-two.

A cave in Mina, outside Mecca. A small group sits with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, one of his companions, later remembered it: a new surah was coming down, and the Prophet was reciting it, and Ibn Mas'ud was taking it fresh from his mouth. Then a snake slid out of the rock. The Prophet told them to kill it. They rushed it, and it got away. And he said, more or less: it was spared your harm, as you were spared its harm. That's how al-Mursalat arrived, in a hadith in al-Bukhari. Surah seventy-seven. It opens with something that keeps coming.

Wal-mursalati 'urfa. By those sent forth, one after another. Al-mursalat comes from the root r-s-l, to send. It's the same root as rasul, a messenger, and risalah, a message. So the very first word of the surah is about sending. But sent forth what? The verse doesn't name them, and the commentators read it in more than one way. Some say the winds, gust after gust. Others say angels, sent down with Allah's commands. Some held both together. And 'urfan has two readings as well. One is one after another, like the hairs of a horse's mane, which is also called 'urf, lying in a row. The other is with kindness, from the same letters as ma'ruf, the good and decent thing. Then come five oaths in a run: those sent forth, those that blow hard, those that spread, those that separate, those that bring down a reminder. Five lines that sound like weather rolling in. And verse six says why the reminder comes: as an excuse or a warning. Verse seven lands the point: what you are promised will surely happen. Notice the pattern. Before the surah says anything about the Day to come, it points at something you've felt on your face. Wind doesn't arrive once. It keeps coming. The surah treats that as a sign: the One who keeps sending the wind keeps sending reminders too. Umm al-Fadl, the Prophet's aunt by marriage, said in another hadith that al-Mursalat was the last surah she heard him recite, at the sunset prayer, near the end of his life. A surah about things that keep coming, and it kept being recited to the end.

The practice: notice one thing that keeps coming. Sit where you are. Close your eyes or lower them. Listen first. Is there something that repeats? A fan, traffic, a clock, wind against a window, a neighbor's footsteps. If the room is silent, there's still one: your breath. In, out, and in again, without your asking. Pick one and stay with it. Each time it comes back, let it count as one more arrival. You don't have to name it as anything else. Just notice that it keeps being sent. The bell holds the time.
Al-mursalat. Those sent forth, one after another: angels or winds, the first word of surah seventy-seven, from the root of messenger. Today's word.
Your line: sent forth. Today, when a gust of wind or a repeated sound catches you, let it be a small reminder that arrived on time. Day six hundred sixty-two.

663.title: Woe that day
663.hook: the refrain repeated ten times: woe that day to the deniers (77:15)
663.howItsDone: Al-Mursalat is recited in prayer and in personal reading; its refrain returns ten times, and commentators read each return against the sign that comes just before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-mursalat, and your line: sent forth. What kept arriving for you, wind, breath, a sound? Today, the second half of al-Mursalat, and the last day of this stretch of the book. Day six hundred sixty-three.

Some songs are built on a chorus. The verse changes, the story moves, and then the same line comes back, and by the third time the listener is waiting for it. Earlier this year, ar-Rahman did that with a question, which of your Lord's favors will you deny, again and again. Al-Mursalat does it too, with a shorter line and a heavier one. It comes back ten times in fifty verses, and the whole surah is built around it.

Surah seventy-seven, verse fifteen, in Pickthall's translation: "Woe unto the repudiators on that day!" In Arabic, waylun yawma'idhin lil-mukadhdhibin. Wayl is woe, a cry of ruin. Yawma'idhin, on that day, the Day the surah has been describing. And al-mukadhdhibin comes from the root k-dh-b, to lie. The form here means more than people who doubt. It's people who call a true thing a lie, who look at it and say, that's false. Pickthall's old word, repudiators, catches that: people who disown what's in front of them. Now watch where the refrain falls. It doesn't only follow scenes of the end. Again and again it follows a gift. Did We not create you from a humble fluid, and shape you? Woe that day to the deniers. Did We not make the earth a place that holds the living and the dead, and set firm mountains on it, and give you sweet water to drink? Woe that day to the deniers. The warning keeps landing right after something good. Some commentators read it that way: the denial in view isn't only of the Day, but of the gifts that point to it. To be handed water, a body, solid ground, and call the giver a fiction. So the refrain works in two directions. It's a warning about the end. And it's a nudge about this afternoon: what good thing in front of you have you been quietly treating as nothing?

The practice: deny nothing good today. Sit, and take an honest inventory of the last day. Look for one good thing you brushed off. A compliment you waved away. A meal someone made that you ate standing up. A message you meant to answer. A morning you woke up healthy and didn't notice. Hold it for a moment. Don't argue with it. Just let it be what it was: a good thing, given. If more come, let them come. The bell holds the time.
Al-mukadhdhibin. Woe that day to the deniers, said ten times in al-Mursalat, often right after a gift: water, body, ground. Today's word.

Your line: don't deny it. This stretch ran from the scattering winds through the balance, which of his favors, a house near you, al-Qalam, constant in prayer and adhkar, to here. Today, when something good arrives, accept it out loud. Day six hundred sixty-three.

664.title: Twenty-five named prophets
664.hook: the Qur'an names twenty-five prophets, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ
664.howItsDone: The twenty-five prophets named in the Qur'an are taught as a list in Islamic schooling, and Muslims add "peace be upon him" (alayhi as-salam) after each prophet's name.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed al-Mursalat with al-mukadhdhibin, and your line: don't deny it. Did you accept one good thing out loud? Today a new stretch begins: the whole book in view, gathered by theme. Day six hundred sixty-four.

Since the start of this year, the path has walked the Qur'an surah by surah, from the Opening to the edge of its last part. Now it steps back. The next weeks hold the book up like a map, and trace the roads that run all the way through it. The first road is people. Open the book and, again and again, someone is there: a man building an ark, a boy in a well, a father on a mountain with his son. Count the prophets the Qur'an names, by the usual reckoning, and you get twenty-five.

The word is nabi, a prophet. Arabic lexicons connect it to naba', news: a nabi is one who receives news from Allah and passes it on. Some link it to a root meaning to be raised up. Beside it stands rasul, a messenger. One explanation scholars give: every messenger is a prophet, but not every prophet was sent with a new message or law. Here are the twenty-five names. Adam. Idris. Nuh. Hud. Salih. Ibrahim. Lut. Isma'il. Ishaq. Ya'qub. Yusuf. Ayyub. Shu'ayb. Musa. Harun. Dhul-Kifl. Dawud. Sulayman. Ilyas. Al-Yasa'. Yunus. Zakariyya. Yahya. 'Isa. And Muhammad ﷺ, called the seal of the prophets in surah thirty-three. Eighteen of them appear in one passage alone, in al-An'am, chapter six, one name after another. Some will sound familiar from the Bible: Noah, Abraham, Moses, David, John, Jesus. Hud and Salih, sent to the Arabian peoples of 'Ad and Thamud, have no counterpart there. And the list isn't the whole family. The Qur'an says plainly that some messengers' stories it has told, and some it has not. A report in Musnad Ahmad puts the number of prophets in the tens of thousands, though scholars debate its chain. The Qur'an also tells believers to say: we make no distinction between any of His messengers. And a hadith in al-Bukhari gives the picture behind today's line. The Prophet said the prophets are brothers with different mothers and one religion. Different times, different peoples, one family.

The practice: say all the names you know. Sit comfortably. Start at the beginning, with Adam, and say each prophet's name you can remember, quietly or in your head, slowly, one per breath. Don't worry about the order or the gaps. When you get stuck, pause on the last name and recall one thing about him: an ark, a well, a staff, a whale. Muslims customarily add peace be upon him after each name; if that's your practice, add it. The bell holds the time.
Nabi. A prophet, one who brings news from Allah. Twenty-five are named in the Qur'an, from Adam to Muhammad ﷺ, and more are left unnamed. Today's word.

Your line: they are one family. Today, when you hear one of these names, Noah, Moses, Jesus, Abraham, in a film, a song or a street sign, remember it's one of the twenty-five the Qur'an names. Day six hundred sixty-four.

665.title: The angels
665.hook: Jibril who brings revelation, Mika'il, Israfil, the recorders on each shoulder
665.howItsDone: Muslims count belief in angels among the pillars of faith; at the end of each prayer they turn the head to the right and then the left with the greeting of peace, which some scholars say includes the angels.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nabi, the prophets, and your line: they are one family. How many names did you find? Today, the ones who carried the news to them. Day six hundred sixty-five, the end of a week.

Watch the end of a Muslim prayer. After the last sitting, the person praying turns their head to the right and says, peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, the same words. If they're praying alone in an empty room, they still turn. Who are they greeting? Partly the people beside them, if there are any. And, some scholars say, someone who's always there: the angels. Today, the mala'ikah.

Mala'ikah is the plural; one angel is a malak. Some lexicons link it to a root for sending a message, and the Qur'an opens surah thirty-five by calling the angels messengers, with wings, two, three and four. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says they were created from light. In the hadith of Jibril, in Sahih Muslim, belief in them is one of the pillars of faith. A few are named. Jibril, Gabriel, brings the revelation down; the Qur'an names him in al-Baqarah, verse ninety-seven, as the one who brought it to the heart of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Mika'il, Michael, is named once, in the very next verse. Tradition connects him with rain and provision. Israfil isn't named in the Qur'an at all. The Qur'an speaks of the trumpet that will be blown on the last Day, and the hadith tradition gives the angel of the trumpet the name Israfil. Then come the ones closest to daily life. Surah fifty says two receivers sit, one on the right and one on the left, and not a word is spoken without a watcher ready. Surah eighty-two calls them kiraman katibin: noble ones, writing, who know what you do. Some scholars teach that the one on the right records the good, and the one on the left the bad. And there's a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim that says when someone intends a good deed and doesn't do it, it's still written as one good deed. Intending a bad one and holding back is written as a good deed too. The ones who write, it turns out, are generous with the pen.
screen: `ONE ON THE RIGHT, ONE ON THE LEFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: greet the angels on your right and left. Sit upright. Take a few slow breaths. Then turn your head gently to the right, and if you'd like, say the words of the prayer's end: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Or simply let the greeting be silent. Turn back to center and breathe. Then turn to the left and do the same. Sit with the thought that whatever you said and did today was seen, and that a good intention counted, even the ones you didn't finish. The bell holds the time.
Mala'ikah. Angels, messengers of light: Jibril with revelation, Mika'il, Israfil with the trumpet, and the noble writers on the right and left. Today's word.

Your line: the ones who write. This week ran from once, nothing, through no thanks wanted, adhkar, sent forth, don't deny it and they are one family. Today, give the writers on your right one good intention to record. Day six hundred sixty-five.

myth: Israfil is named in the Qur'an
the Qur'an mentions the trumpet; the name Israfil comes from the hadith tradition.
a good deed intended but not done is still written
a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim says it counts as one good deed.
the Qur'an describes angels with wings
surah thirty-five: wings, two, three and four.

fork.setup: you meant to call a sick friend today, and the day ran out. according to the hadith, what do the writers on your right record?
options: one good deed, for the intention.
fork.reveal: the hadith says a good intention not carried out is written as one good deed; carried out, it's multiplied.

trapdoor: what you thought: angels are winged figures in paintings.
what it means: mala'ikah are messengers made of light: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and two noble writers beside each person.
what a scholar hears: Mika'il is named only in 2:98; Israfil's name comes from hadith, not the Qur'an; 50:17–18 places the recorders right and left.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 8 (the hadith of Jibril: belief in the angels)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6491; Sahih Muslim 131 (good intentions recorded)
